The 2023 previous disclosures D059 and D060 separately describe the increases in R&D expense and SG&A expense, respectively, both attributed to compensation and employee growth. These form the component parts of the 2024 consolidated discussion.

current_disclosures.summary: Research and development expenses and sales, general, and administrative expenses increased in fiscal year 2024, primarily driven by compensation and benefits, including stock-based compensation, which reflected employee growth and compensation increases.

materiality_analysis.reason: The change is primarily a structural reorganization of the disclosure, combining R&D and SG&A expenses into a single narrative rather than separate lines. The underlying drivers (compensation, employee growth) remain consistent and are not new risks or strategic shifts. The consolidation of the explanation does not materially change the substance of the expense increases.
materiality_analysis.key_change: Consolidation of R&D and SG&A expense narratives

current_disclosures.summary: Research and development expenses for fiscal year 2025 increased, driven by a 32% rise in compensation and benefits, a 100% increase in compute and infrastructure costs, and a 234% increase in engineering development costs for new product introductions.

comparisons.peer_topic: R&D Expense Increase and AI Headcount
comparisons.peer_summary: AMD's research and development expenses increased by 10% to $6.5 billion in 2024, primarily driven by higher employee-related costs resulting from an increase in headcount to support the company's AI strategy.
comparisons.comparison: Both NVDA and AMD attribute increases in their Research and Development (R&D) expenses primarily to higher employee compensation and headcount growth. NVDA states that R&D and SG&A increases were "primarily driven by compensation and benefits, including stock-based compensation, reflecting employee growth and compensation increases." Similarly, AMD reports that its R&D expense increase "was primarily due to higher employee-related costs due to an increase in headcount in support of our AI strategy."

sentences.text: The increase in research and development expenses and sales, general and administrative expenses for fiscal year 2024 was primarily driven by compensation and benefits, including stock-based compensation, reflecting employee growth and compensation increases.
The increase was primarily due to higher employee-related costs due to an increase in headcount in support of our AI strategy.

comparisons.peer_summary: Marketing, general and administrative expenses were $2.8 billion in 2024, an increase of $431 million or 18% from $2.4 billion in 2023, primarily due to increased go-to-market activities supporting revenue growth.
comparisons.comparison: While NVDA combines R&D and SG&A drivers into a single explanation centered on compensation and employee growth, AMD separates these expenses with distinct drivers. AMD's SG&A increase is attributed to "go-to-market activities to support our revenue growth," whereas NVDA's combined increase is linked to compensation. This highlights a difference in operational focus: NVDA's expense growth is cost/compensation-led, while AMD's SG&A growth is revenue/activity-led.

sentences.text: The increase in research and development expenses and sales, general and administrative expenses for fiscal year 2024 was primarily driven by compensation and benefits, including stock-based compensation, reflecting employee growth and compensation increases.
The increase was primarily due to an increase in go-to-market activities to support our revenue growth.

comparisons.peer_summary: Research and development expense increased by $4,057 million (77%) in fiscal year 2024 compared to the prior year, primarily driven by higher compensation and headcount resulting from the VMware Merger, as well as higher stock-based compensation expense from annual equity awards granted at higher grant-date fair values.
comparisons.comparison: Both companies cite higher compensation, stock-based compensation, and headcount increases as primary drivers for rising R&D expenses. NVDA notes R&D increases were "driven by compensation and benefits, including stock-based compensation, reflecting employee growth." AVGO reports R&D increases were "primarily due to higher compensation, including higher stock-based compensation, as a result of an increase in headcount from the VMware Merger." Both explicitly link stock-based compensation and headcount to expense growth.
